Lab guide

1. Observe the changing view

You are operating a fictional wide-field telescope. The space telescope uses Hubble images of Jupiter from January 5–6, 2024, combined with calculated moon positions. It is not a sequence of real Hubble exposures of all four moons. The default campaign starts at that image epoch. Ground-based mode adds adjustable atmospheric blur and optional cloudy sessions.

Choose a start date and observation interval. Explore the motion with Play motion and Overhead view, then pause and return to Telescope view to take measurements. An orbit seen nearly edge-on looks like motion back and forth.

2. Build an observing record

Hover over a fuzzy spot to identify the moon, then click its center to record immediately. Clicking that moon again at the same time replaces its measurement, preserving its inclusion setting and note. The exact pixel you click sets your measurement; it is not snapped to the predicted position. Left and right arrow keys move between observations while the telescope has focus. The same controls sit beside the observing date. Use Undo recording (or Ctrl/Command+Z) to undo the last recording, including a replacement. Repeat for all four moons when visible. A typical CLEA exercise uses 18 successful sessions at 12-hour intervals. Longer coverage is helpful for Callisto. In ground-based mode, cloudy sessions and moons hidden by Jupiter create genuine gaps; do not record missing positions as zero.

If moons overlap or a click is ambiguous, the nearby chooser offers each moon and Both (or All for a larger group). Both records the same clicked coordinate for each moon. The observer decides whether to use the blend; every recorded point can be independently included or excluded from its fit. No measurement changes until an assignment is chosen.

Brightness and contrast change the display of a retained image. Raising brightness can wash out Jupiter and reveal glare near its limb, hiding nearby moons. Reset image restores the original display. These controls do not change positions or previously recorded measurements.

If names are hidden, assign the moon yourself in Manual assignment below the image. Automatic recording is available when identification and distance readout are enabled. If distances are hidden, use Measure scale to measure Jupiter’s diameter in detector pixels. Its center is x = 500; compute the moon’s east-positive position as (500 − moon x) / Jupiter’s pixel diameter. The displayed sensor is always 1000 × 360 virtual pixels, regardless of your screen size.

3. Estimate and fit an orbit

Start with Callisto, then Ganymede, Europa, and Io. The largest east/west displacement estimates A; a full repeat estimates P. Choose t₀ where the curve crosses zero toward positive (east). Enter your estimates, plot the curve, and adjust the sliders while watching the graph and RMS residual.

Refine fit searches close to your initial period and adjusts amplitude and phase. It cannot guarantee the correct period with sparse observations. Look for alternative cycle counts, especially for Io. Excluded points remain visible. Use a limited time range if appropriate, and explain exclusions in your notes.

4. Determine the mass

The fit amplitude is an orbital radius, expressed in Jupiter diameters. Convert it to a physical radius and apply M ≈ 4π²a³/(GP²), neglecting the moon’s mass and treating the orbit as circular. Compare your four estimates. The mean shown is an unweighted summary, not an uncertainty estimate.

5. Keep the evidence

Save session downloads all settings, observations, fits, and notes. Open session restores that file. Export CSV saves one file with elapsed time in days followed by Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto positions in Jupiter diameters (east positive). In Data Tool, load the CSV, use elapsed time as X, and choose the moon column as Y. Missing positions stay blank. UTC, Julian date, inclusion flags, notes and overlap assignments follow as metadata; review exclusions and fit intervals in Data Tool, since CSV does not transfer those settings automatically. Save PNG and Print report ask for lab group members and offer all four moons in one figure or the current moon alone. The figure includes a report timestamp, observing epoch, recorded points, saved curves, periods, amplitudes, zero crossings, Jupiter masses and RMS residuals. Figures use the full recorded time interval. Print includes only the figure and its analysis. This app does not send students’ measurements to a class database.

Questions to investigate

Why does the projected motion resemble a sine wave? What happens if observations always sample similar phases? Which affects the inferred mass more: a 10% error in radius or period? How would a more distant moon’s period compare?

Model, sources & limitations

This independently implemented educational reconstruction follows the observing and analysis workflow in Project CLEA’s The Revolution of the Moons of Jupiter. It is not the original CLEA executable.

Orbital positions

Uses the bundled, MIT-licensed Astronomy Engine 2.1.19. Jovicentric moon positions are projected into Jupiter’s equatorial east–west direction, as seen from Earth’s center, with the Earth–Jupiter light-travel delay. The overhead view is a projection onto Jupiter’s equatorial plane at the same emission time.

CLEA’s technical manual describes a different, low-accuracy Meeus model. Exact numerical agreement with the Windows software has not been established. This application is a teaching simulation, not an eclipse-timing or telescope-planning service.

Observing simplifications

The telescope uses physical moon diameters with approximate relative reflectance, softened by the same optical blur as Jupiter. The optical image is retained as 32-bit floating-point linear RGB before a display stretch. Brightness and contrast change only that stretch. Jupiter has a fixed illustrative scattered-light halo that becomes more visible when brightened. The Hubble texture remains a processed source image, not raw CCD counts; photometry, noise and detector saturation are not calibrated. Jupiter hides far-side moons, including during partial limb crossings. Front-side moons cover the clouds beneath them; their computed shadows are separate dark spots. Eclipse visibility uses a simplified Jupiter umbra, and shadow locations use parallel sunlight intersecting an oblate planet. Mutual moon events, penumbrae, local horizon, daylight, exposure noise and sky brightness are not modeled. This is not suitable for precise contact or eclipse timing. Ground-based seeing is an illustrative Gaussian blur, with its arcsecond setting referenced to a nominal 40-arcsecond Jupiter. Clicking records your selected detector coordinate rather than substituting an exact orbital position. The optional keyboard target buttons use the nearest whole detector pixel to the predicted center.

Catalog background stars

The background uses real stars from the Tycho-2 main catalogue and Supplement-1 (Høg et al. 2000, A&A 355, L27; CDS/VizieR I/259). A five-degree band on either side of the J2000 ecliptic is retained through Tycho VT magnitude 12. Catalog positions are propagated using linear proper motion to the observing date, then projected relative to Jupiter’s date-dependent geocentric position and angular diameter. Stars without proper motion retain their catalog position. This is a magnitude-limited catalog, not a complete faint sky; annual stellar parallax, variable-star brightness and binary orbital motion are omitted. Star magnitudes use VT as an approximate relative brightness. Catalog subset and provenance.

Jupiter image sequence & credits

Nine unretouched planet images from the January 2024 Hubble OPAL release supply Jupiter’s appearance. Views 04–06, containing Io or its shadow, are excluded. Each image is aligned by the planet’s center and diameter, clipped to the disk, scaled and blurred at runtime. The nearest available rotational aspect repeats on a 9.925-hour cycle. The release’s timestamp labels are treated as UTC for approximate visual phase only; this is not an absolute longitude calibration. Jupiter’s photographed phase and cloud weather are illustrative outside the source epoch, and the image changes in discrete steps.

Full image credit: NASA, ESA, Amy Simon (NASA-GSFC); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI). ESA/Hubble release · Reuse policy · CC BY 4.0 · Per-image source record. Simulated moons, shadows and blur are adaptations; NASA/ESA do not endorse this app.

Constants and analysis

Uses Jupiter’s equatorial diameter 142,984 km, AU = 149,597,870.7 km, a Julian year of 365.25 days, G = 6.67430 × 10⁻¹¹ SI, and Earth mass 5.9722 × 10²⁴ kg. The viewing direction changes as Earth and Jupiter move, so an apparent fitted period can differ slightly from a sidereal orbital period. Sine fitting assumes circular orbits; small departures from a sine curve can be physical as well as measurement errors. Refine fit performs unweighted local least squares. Formal parameter uncertainties are not estimated.

The original worksheet uses rounded conversions (1,050 Jupiter diameters per AU and 365 days per year); these modern constants can produce small systematic differences.
